passages.t: The prophets speak, and the building begins again
passages.happening:
‘Later, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo prophesied to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel, who was over them’ (verse 1). So Zerubbabel and Jeshua ‘rose up and began to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem. And the prophets of God were with them, helping them’ (verse 2).

Soon the Persian officials arrive. Tattenai, the governor of the region west of the Euphrates, comes with Shethar-bozenai and their associates and asks, “Who authorized you to rebuild this temple and restore this structure?” (verse 3). They also ask, “What are the names of the men who are constructing this building?” (verse 4).

‘But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, so that they were not stopped until a report was sent to Darius and written instructions about this matter were returned’ (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Darius I seized the Persian throne in 522 BC after a time of revolt, and he spent his first years putting down rebellions across the empire. His second year was 520 BC. That year the word of the LORD came through Haggai, and within weeks the work began again. Zechariah began to prophesy two months later. Their messages, kept in their own books, rebuked the people for living in finished houses while God's house lay in ruins, and promised that God was with them.

The work restarts because prophets speak, not because the danger has passed. Chapter 4 ended with the work standing still. Chapter 5 opens with that stillness broken by the word of God.

Tattenai was the governor of the large Persian province west of the Euphrates, of which Judah was a small part. A Babylonian document from the reign of Darius names a Tattannu as governor of that province, very likely the same man. His questions are the questions of a careful official. Building a temple or a fortification needed royal permission, and after the revolts at the start of Darius's reign, an unexplained building project in a city with a history of rebellion would call for a report. Taking down names meant that someone could be held to account.

Then the hinge of the chapter: the eye of their God. The Persian official is watching. But God is watching more closely, and the work goes on while the letter travels.
passages.later:
Haggai's first word to the people was a question: “Is it a time for you yourselves to live in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?” (Haggai 1:4). Then the same verb that opens Ezra comes back: ‘So the LORD stirred the spirit of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah’ (Haggai 1:14).

The eye of God on his people is a picture the psalms use for his care: ‘Surely the eyes of the LORD are on those who fear Him’ (Psalm 33:18).
passages.asks: The work began again because God's word was spoken, not because the danger was gone. Ask what has stalled in your life, and whether you have been waiting for the circumstances to change before you move. And ask who stands beside you, as the prophets stood beside the builders, helping.

passages.t: The governor's report to the king
passages.happening:
Tattenai and his associates send King Darius a report. It begins, ‘To King Darius: All peace’ (verse 7).

‘Let it be known to the king that we went into the province of Judah, to the house of the great God. The people are rebuilding it with large stones, and placing timbers in the walls. This work is being carried out diligently and is prospering in their hands’ (verse 8).

They report that they asked the elders who had authorized the work, and that they asked for the names of the leaders, ‘so that we could write down the names of their leaders for your information’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
This letter is very different from the letter of chapter 4. There, officials accused Jerusalem and urged the king to stop the work. Here a governor asks his questions, describes what he saw, and passes the matter up to the king. He even calls the temple ‘the house of the great God’ (verse 8) and says that the work is prospering.

The building method he describes, with courses of timber laid between courses of stone, is a known ancient technique. It is the method described for the inner court of Solomon's temple, and it is in Cyrus's own instructions for this temple (6:4).

Like the rest of this section, the chapter is in Aramaic, and most of it is a letter quoted in full. The elders of the Jews are the community's leaders before the Persian authorities. The Aramaic word for them means the gray-haired, and it reflects the old pattern of leadership in Israel by the heads of families and clans, which carried on under foreign rule.
passages.later: Solomon had built in the same way: ‘Solomon built the inner courtyard with three rows of dressed stone and one row of trimmed cedar beams’ (1 Kings 6:36).
passages.asks: Tattenai asked hard questions and reported what he saw. Ask how you respond when someone in authority asks you to account for what you are doing. And ask whether your own work could stand an honest report.

passages.t: The elders' answer, and a search of the archives
passages.happening:
The report gives the elders' answer in their own words. “We are servants of the God of heaven and earth, and we are rebuilding the temple that was built many years ago, which a great king of Israel built and completed” (verse 11).

They tell the temple's story. ‘But since our fathers angered the God of heaven, He delivered them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon’ (verse 12), who destroyed the temple and carried the people away. Then, they say, ‘In his first year, however, Cyrus king of Babylon issued a decree to rebuild this house of God’ (verse 13). Cyrus gave the temple's gold and silver articles to a man named Sheshbazzar, whom he made governor, and Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundation. “From that time until now it has been under construction, but it has not yet been completed” (verse 16).

Tattenai ends by asking the king to search the royal archives in Babylon, ‘to see if King Cyrus did indeed issue a decree to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem’ (verse 17), and to send his decision.
passages.hearers:
The elders' answer is a short history of the temple: Solomon's house, the people's sin, Nebuchadnezzar's destruction, Cyrus's decree, the return of the vessels and the foundation laid. Through the voice of a Persian official, the reader hears the book's own account of the past.

The answer is honest. Before a foreign official, the elders confess that their fathers angered God and that the exile was the result. They do not say that their God failed to protect his temple. They say that he handed it over. They own their past instead of excusing it, and then they appeal to the law of the empire, Cyrus's decree.

Cyrus is called king of Babylon here, because after 539 BC he ruled it. And the elders name Sheshbazzar as the one who laid the foundation, where chapter 3 names Zerubbabel and Jeshua. The notes on chapter 3 set out how readers have put the accounts together.

The chapter ends in suspense. The letter goes to Darius, and the reader must wait until chapter 6 to learn what the archives will show.
passages.later:
The elders' honesty runs through the great prayers after the exile. In Nehemiah the people pray, ‘You are just in all that has befallen us, because You have acted faithfully, while we have acted wickedly’ (Nehemiah 9:33).

The great king who built and completed the first temple was Solomon: ‘So Solomon built the temple and finished it’ (1 Kings 6:14).
passages.asks: The elders told a foreign official the truth about their own past, without excuses. Ask whether you can speak as honestly about the failures in your own story, and in your church's story. And ask what you would say if someone asked you who you are, and why you are building what you build.
